Alright. So here is a skip whose primary food source is kids. Changing this:

Following an investigation by the Ethics Committee, containment protocols have been adjusted to no longer include providing live human prey for SCP-974 as of 01/01/201█. An increased stock of small animals typical for the environment will be introduced in order to provide sustenance for SCP-974.

To this:

Following an investigation by the Ethics Committee, containment protocols have been adjusted to no longer include providing live human prey for SCP-974 as of 01/01/201█. Attempts to use SCP-1680 instances as a substitute have failed following SCP-974 rejection of all instances it has been presented with. An increased stock of small animals typical for the environment will be introduced in order to provide sustenance for SCP-974.

If anyone has other/better examples that could be used here please leave a comment saying so!

item.title: (no title)
item.content:encoded:
After reading this article alone, my first thought was, "Okay, so it starts growing when it stops getting its preferred food? Is that even supposed to make sense?" Now that I've read all the discussion, I can see it making sense, but there's another problem that bothered me both before and after reading the discussion: "Things what we better do what they want cuz we won't like them when they're mad" is also on the list of clichés, so this technically uses two clichés to justify containment procedures that are already over the top. The SCP is good. The "contain it by feeding it children" is good. The reason for the "contain it by feeding it children" is bad. If some reason why it needs to be contained and fed children could be devised that isn't cliché or phoned in, this would be a great article.

And because I don't like making ultimatums like that without offering some suggestions:

First of all, to answer the people who ask "why don't we just kill it?", take the bit where a bunch more were found in the wild after they killed the first one that went into "puberty" and make it so that those new ones in the wild happened because the Foundation killed the first one - you would also be answering the question of "how do they reproduce?" Yes, the Foundation killed all but one of the new ones with no apparent adverse effects, but there are several ways that could be worked around without removing it: They didn't multiply because one of them was still alive, they did multiply but far away from wherever the Foundation was looking for them, etc.

Second of all, because I like the "eternal youth" theory that people have been suggesting, keep the monstrous "adult" form of the creature, but try to take it from "superpowered monstrosity" to "tragic monstrosity" (admittedly, this is done a lot on this site, but it's more acceptable than the clichés on the Big List because it doesn't just appeal to human instinct [oh god it's a big scary monster that will kill us all!], it also hits readers right in the feels, you know?). What I would do is this: Make the "juvenile" form of this monster sapient instead of just sentient - only the "juvenile" form, mind, keep the "adult" form as-is; make it aware of what will happen if it doesn't stay young by eating children; and make it not want to "grow up", specifically because of the widespread destruction it would cause.

Anyway, that's all I've got. Neutral vote for promising idea but sub-par execution.

item.content:encoded:
How can you secure, contain, and protect some mysterious dimension/structure/etc if you haven't explored it?

"Oh, hey. This door opens to a hallway that doesn't fit into reality. I think I hear something moving around back there, too."
"Just bolt it up and hang a 'Do Not Disturb' sign on it. I'm sure that'll do it."

In my mind, the Foundation will study an SCP until 1 of 2 things occurs:

  1. They're no longer uncovering any new information.
  2. Going any further becomes far too dangerous.

After all, if they had never done vigorous testing on SCP-093 they may never have discovered its mirror-portal properties. If they then subsequently didn't explore the alternate Earth they never would have learned that SCP-093 is not unique, and other stones might pose a security threat.

item.content:encoded:
My real problem here is that we're not studying this thing at all. What've we learnt of it? Anything we can use?

To me, that's not a problem at all. In my head canon, To Secure, Contain, and Protect means that the anomalous subject is contained, the subject is secured (not exposed to danger or harm) and the subject is protected. If the subject is kept contained and safe, i.e. preserved by feeding it with kids, then that's what they do. The Foundation just contains, that's it. The only thing they need to learn is how to contain it and keep it safe. They don't need to learn anything else, they don't need to study it, no "greater good" or anything useful does not need to come out of it. They just contain, simple as that.

Consequently, this is also why I've never much liked articles that rely heavily on explorations. All that the Foundation needs to know is how to contain an anomaly and keep it safe. Anything that could be of use in something else is none of their concern. To me, SCP does not mean Silly experiments, Cool adventures, and Pointless explorations.

item.content:encoded:
I'm going to disagree with your argument but agree with your point. The Foundation shouldn't be feeding these things kids. Not because they don't have the capability, the capacity, or the willingness to do so-they probably do-but because that makes the article about how the Foundation is a pack of boogeymen, instead of about the thing itself. The conceit and the fact that they exist in the wild is enough to justify keeping an open file on them; tying one to a stake in the backyard only serves to blur the focus here.

As far as the puberty phase thing goes, I think it works in some ways and doesn't in others. With or without it you've got a kind of very grim joke about the eternal boy archetype, the cannibilization and perpetuation of youth embodied as a poisonous, destructive obsession that destroys the very innocence that youth is made of. (As a tangent, I think having the SCP prefer to scavenge its nests out of discarded toys, clothes, and the beloved pop culture paraphernalia of our own childhoods would make that a bit more bitingly topical, though, admittedly, also super blunt.) But with the puberty stage it takes on a melancholy aspect of misremembered youth and the inevitable disappointments of growing up, and without that it becomes a more static commentary on our own cultural affinity for self-infantilization and our inability to let the past go. In other words, I think it tips the article between IT and acidly mocking VH-1's I Love The 80's.

item.content:encoded: I like how strongly it starts out, but as it goes on, the sheer weight of "we're feeding it because…" starts to wear on it. The concept is very strong, though I have to say I feel as though, even for the Foundation, it would be a logistical nightmare to carry out the feeding. Granted, the Foundation is bound to go to extraordinary lengths to keep indescribable horror contained, but the feeding children thing feels a bit like a forced element to the creepiness of something that was pretty creepy and relatable to begin with. For something that seems so benign, the lengths the containment goes to seem slightly absurd. I agree with the previous posts that suggest some sort of further reason to keep the entity contained; otherwise we're just keeping it alive for its own sake. Not to suggest destruction or anything so drastic, but perhaps some reasoning behind the protocol and the need for such a high price to be paid for its containment; this seems to tread the line between the Foundation sacrificing things for the greater good and a sort of malevolence, at least considering how many other horrible SCPs are kept in check using far less than horrible means. The treehouse concept is good, the child-eating is good, I'd say it needs to go somewhere else to make it genuinely weird, something to play more on that fear in the beginning when you tap into that fear of "I've seen one of those when I was younger…" and keep it going.
